node.label: Patricia Seed
node.date_label: To Love, Honor, and Obey (1988) · Ceremonies of Possession (1995) · American Pentimento (2001) · AHR transnational conversation (2006)
node.description: In Ceremonies of Possession in Europe’s Conquest of the New World, 1492–1640 (1995), Patricia Seed argued that European claims to the Americas drew authority from distinct cultural practices. She compared English, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Dutch ways of making possession legitimate through familiar actions, language and technical knowledge. John A. Crider welcomed its bridge between literary and historical inquiry but questioned the strength of its national patterns and the comparability of its cases. To Love, Honor, and Obey in Colonial Mexico (1988) examined changing meanings of love, free will and honor in marriage disputes. Kimberly Gauderman discussed objections to its representativeness while defending its study of competing discourses. Her “Colonial and Postcolonial Discourse” (1991) prompted responses from Hernán Vidal, Rolena Adorno and Walter Mignolo in Latin American Research Review; she answered them in “More Colonial and Postcolonial Discourses” (1993). She also contributed to the six-person AHR conversation on transnational history (2006).
node.representative_figures_and_works: To Love, Honor, and Obey in Colonial Mexico: Conflicts over Marriage Choice, 1574–1821 (1988); “Failing to Marvel” (1991); “Colonial and Postcolonial Discourse” (1991); Ceremonies of Possession in Europe’s Conquest of the New World, 1492–1640 (1995); American Pentimento: The Invention of Indians and the Pursuit of Riches (2001); “AHR Conversation: On Transnational History” (2006), with C. A. Bayly, Sven Beckert, Matthew Connelly, Isabel Hofmeyr and Wendy Kozol.
node.scope_note: Selected primary passages in the two 1991 articles and the 2006 conversation read; complete 1993 reply and two named reviews read. Ceremonies of Possession and To Love, Honor, and Obey not read in full. American Pentimento front matter only; its argument is not summarized here. Bhabha’s underlying text and Derrida’s and Said’s cited books unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Colonial and Postcolonial Discourse” (1991), Seed criticizes Orientalism (1978) for omitting non-Western texts and asserting rather than demonstrating how knowledge became power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 189 and 192: “affirmed rather than demonstrated.” Qualified methodological criticism; Said’s book and reply unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Colonial and Postcolonial Discourse” (1991), Seed develops Bhabha’s account of an addressed colonial discourse by adding its enforcement through coercive institutions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 184 n. 7: “To Bhabha’s proposition, I would add.” Specific conceptual use; Bhabha’s underlying text unidentified and unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Failing to Marvel” (1991), Seed uses Derrida’s critique of Lévi-Strauss to question the cultural superiority attributed to alphabetic writing.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 8, text and n. 4, citing “The Violence of the Letter” in Of Grammatology (English translation 1976; French original 1967). Derrida’s book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Seed and C. A. Bayly were co-participants and credited coauthors of “AHR Conversation: On Transnational History” (2006).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read participant heading and pp. 1441–1443. Six-person published collaboration, not agreement or a separately documented two-person collaboration.

proposed_edges.relationship: Seed and Sven Beckert were co-participants and credited coauthors of “AHR Conversation: On Transnational History” (2006).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read participant heading and pp. 1441–1446. Six-person published collaboration; their individual positions remain distinct.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Colonial and Postcolonial Discourse” (1991) synthesizes an interdisciplinary critique of colonial language, representation and authority.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 182–185 and 198–199: “interdisciplinary critique.” Contribution to debate, not a claim of founding the field.

proposed_edges.relationship: Crider’s 1996 review reads Ceremonies of Possession (1995) as connecting cultural interpretation with histories of colonial power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Review, opening and EVALUATION, especially paragraph beginning “What distinguishes.” Mediated reading; Crider also questions the book’s national comparisons.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gauderman’s review locates To Love, Honor, and Obey in Colonial Mexico (1988) within family-history debates about marriage choice and patriarchal authority.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Review pp. 114–116: “Family history.” Supports a family-history contribution, not population reconstruction; primary book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Law and Colonial Cultures: Legal Regimes in World History, 1400–1900 (2002), Lauren Benton criticized Patricia Seed’s Ceremonies of Possession in Europe’s Conquest of the New World, 1492–1640 (1995) for overstating differences between European possession practices through comparisons of different symbolic activities, while valuing its comparative approach.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Cambridge University Press’s sample, including the discussion of jurisdictional and cultural boundaries. Note 17 directly evaluates Seed’s comparisons and warns against extrapolating from symbolic possession to mutual incomprehension of legal orders. The surrounding body develops the distinction between initial possession and subsequent legal relations; note 19 also discusses Seed’s argument about messages sent and received. This is substantive critical engagement, not a collective reference. The whole monograph was not read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Doing the Continental’ (1997), Gordon S. Wood drew on Patricia Seed’s Ceremonies of Possession in Europe’s Conquest of the New World, 1492–1640 (1995) to argue that inherited English practices of exclusion constrained later Anglo-American choices, using her comparative findings in his criticism of Lester D. Langley’s account of the American revolutions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The publisher’s review text explicitly uses Seed’s findings to challenge Langley on political choice. This records a specific use; Langley’s book is the work under review.
